newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says pushing hard for U.N. landmine expert.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says pushing hard for U.N. landmine expert.

text.p: The United States said on Wednesday it would push hard for a United Nations special coordinator to work toward a global ban on anti-personnel landmines even if its current attempt failed.
"We believe a special coordinator for that purpose is necessary, and we look forward to working hard toward reaching that goal," State Department spokesman John Dinger told a news briefing.

The United States has been pressing its case for a coordinator at the U.N.-sponsored Conference on Disarmament in Geneva, the forum it contends is best-suited to signing the first global anti-mine treaty.

On Tuesday, the latest U.S. effort to launch the 61-member conference toward a global ban failed to get off the ground, stymied by a lack of consensus. Cuba and Syria, joined by Burma and Morocco, were holding up progress to press their demands for a package that includes nuclear disarmament.

Dinger said the United States hoped the conference would act on the proposal to appoint a special coordinator on Thursday, before the end of its current seven-week session, its second such session this year.
If the effort fails at the session on Thursday, "there is Part III of this year's Conference on Disarmament, which begins in late July. And we will, if necessary, take it to Part III," Dinger said.
A separate fast-track, Canadian-led initiative to ban landmines in the near future, meanwhile, proceeded apace at a conference in Brussels being attended by the United States as an observer.

Belgian diplomats said 62 countries had so far signed a declaration preparing a landmine ban treaty and almost twice as many had promised to do so. The United States has not joined, notably because Russia and China are not taking part in the so-called Ottawa Process, which began last year.

The treaty would be the first to ban the production, use, stockpiling and transfer of anti-personnel landmines. Supporters hope that at least 75 countries will volunteer to sign the treaty when the conference concludes in Ottawa in December.
Dinger said the United States was attending the Ottawa Process meetings because "we believe those processes can be complementary" to the U.N. track.
